newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Armenian leader moves to disarm critics-diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Armenian leader moves to disarm critics-diplomats.

text.p: Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan, facing possible protests to force him from power, has tried to disarm critics by choosing a new prime minister with wide popular appeal, diplomats said.

The 52-year old former Soviet dissident last week named Robert Kocharyan, leader of Azerbaijan's breakaway ethnic Armenian region of Nagorno-Karabakh, as the former Soviet republic's sixth premier in as many years.

The move came as a shock inside and outside the country and observers said it could complicate regional peace efforts. Karabakh, surrounded by Azeri territory but populated by ethnic Armenians, broke from Baku's rule in the late 1980s.

Karabakh has declared indpendence but leaders say full union with Armenia is their ultimate goal. Fighting over the region killed thousands of Christian Armenians and Moslem Azeris before a 1994 ceasefire, but no lasting settlement has been found.
Kocharyan is popular both in the republic and among the powerful Armenian diaspora in western Europe and North America. Diplomats say he might help Ter-Petrosyan deflect criticism.

More importantly he is respected by nationalist and opposition foes of Ter-Petrosyan who allege the president rigged last September's presidential election. Foreign monitors say the vote was marred by irregularities.
"This (appointing Kocharyan) is a brilliant and very bold move by the president," said one Western diplomat in Yerevan.
"Kocharyan is almost a sacred symbol in this country and it will make it all the more difficult for the opposition to criticise Ter-Petrosyan," he said.
Opposition leaders are scheduled to meet on Saturday.
They say one course of action would be to call for massive rallies and civil disobidience to force Ter-Petrosyan to resign or call new elections.
Vazgen Manukyan, a former prime minister who says Ter-Petrosyan cheated to beat him in last year's election, says the government might face a "Belgrade Spring".

Protesters forced changes to local administrations in Belgrade and other parts of Serbia with massive daily rallies after authorities annulled a string of opposition electoral victories in local elections in November.
Diplomats and other observers say they do not know if opposition forces can muster enough strength on the streets to apply sufficient pressure on Ter-Petrosyan to force change.
They add that Kocharyan's appointment may take momentum away from any movement to force him to make concessions.
"He has put this very popular figure in between himself and the opposition. The goal is make critics of the leadership into apostates. It is very clever," said the western diplomat.
"Karabakh is an emotional question for Armenians and Kocharyan is the symbol of that movement."
Kocharyan, 43, is revered by many among the millions of ethnic Armenians living around the world. The diaspora provides vital financial and political support for Armenia.
"Some in the diaspora were very upset with Ter-Petrosyan and he cannot afford to lose their backing. Kocharyan can serve as kind of a foster child for them," said another diplomat.
Observers say it is less clear what effect Kocharyan's appointment will have on the intractable Karabakh conflict.

They say Ter-Petrosyan may also be seeking to bring the position of the Karabakh leadership, which takes a hard line on independence or union, closer to that of Yerevan's, which is believed to be more inclined to compromise with the Azeris.
Ter-Petrosyan is expected to hold talks with Azeri President Haydar Aliyev on the sidelines of Friday's CIS summit in Moscow.
